95b062ae: The ask is the part people avoid. Here is what to say, who to pick, and the terms to agree so it lasts longer than a fortnight.
fdcb265e: How to Ask a Friend to Be Your Accountability Buddy
bfdc6ef2: How do I ask someone to be my accountability partner?
40c4ecdf: Be direct and state the exact time cost. Explain that you have blocked an app, that you will turn the block off yourself unless someone else holds the key, and that their job is to tap approve or deny on a notification. Explicitly tell them they are allowed to say no.
8013bce6: What if my friend says no?
81af2ad8: That is a reasonable answer and not a judgement of you. Ask someone else, or use a lock level that does not need a buddy at all, such as an enforced waiting period. Many people find a five-minute delay is enough on its own.
953940bc: Can my accountability buddy see my screen time?
6a04920c: In Disconnect, no. Your buddy sees only the unlock requests you send, including the rule name and any reason you choose to write. The apps you block, your schedule and your usage statistics never leave your device.
a0285c7a: Should my partner or spouse be my accountability buddy?
22d1d26c: Often not the best choice. Someone who wants to reach you quickly has a built-in reason to approve every request. A sibling, direct friend or respected colleague usually holds the line more reliably.

83505efd: Most people never set up accountability because one small thing feels awkward: asking. It is a smaller ask than you think, and there is a script.
071c2590: By Shuaib Khan · 5 min read · Updated August 2026
5ce952ab: The mechanism is simple and the evidence is good. The barrier is social: admitting to someone that you cannot manage this alone.
1a07c5bc: Two things make that easier. The first is realising how small the ask actually is. The second is having the words ready.
cfb6044a: What you are actually asking for
7d30af70: People imagine they are asking a friend to supervise them. They are not. In a well-built setup the request is:
fe4e2857: "Occasionally your phone will buzz. It will say I am asking to unlock an app. Tap yes or no. That is the entire job."
835d635a: No monitoring. No reports. No check-ins. They will not see which apps you blocked, your schedule, or your usage — only the request when you send one. Total time cost: a few seconds a week, dropping as the habit fades.
f2cf9618: Said plainly, it stops sounding like a burden.
d368e03a: Your buddy does not need an iPhone. If they are on Android, desktop, or tablet, they approve requests through the buddy web app — no install, just an email link. The experience is the same: they get a notification, tap approve or deny, done.
66f36e6a: The best buddy is someone who can decline without discomfort. That usually is not your closest person.
0c936aee: Good picks: a sibling, a direct friend, a colleague you respect, someone with a dry sense of humour about it.
eca95a83: Risky picks: a romantic partner (wants to reach you), your most agreeable friend (will always say yes), someone with the same habit (mutual permission).
7907d3fc: One useful filter: imagine sending them an irritated message at 11pm asking them to just approve it. If you can picture them saying "no, go to bed" and finding it slightly funny, they are the right person.
3563f04d: Short and unembarrassed works best. Something like:
69d0935e: "I'm trying to stop losing my evenings to [app]. I've set it to block, but the only way it actually works is if someone else can approve unlocking it — otherwise I just turn it off myself.
5d5f769b: Would you be that person? You'd get a notification when I request access and tap approve or deny. Nothing else, no monitoring. Takes a second. And you're allowed to say no — that's the whole point."
c891c9f7: Three things make this work: it names the real reason without self-flagellation, it states the exact time cost, and it explicitly gives them permission to refuse.
9a66624d: If you would rather make it mutual
238d6372: Offer to be their buddy too. It removes the asymmetry and makes the ask feel like a shared project. Just avoid pairing on the identical habit — two people quitting the same app tend to approve each other's requests out of fellow feeling.
a48f2363: Agree the terms in the same conversation
682abb69: Five minutes now saves the arrangement later:
6c663ace: What counts as a real reason. A genuine emergency, a specific work need. "I'm bored" is a no. Say this out loud now, while you are calm.
7292bfa1: What to do when you push back. Tell them explicitly: if I argue, that is the craving talking, not new information. Hold the line.
4b95facd: How long an approval lasts. Fifteen minutes to do the thing, not the rest of the evening.
44d43a51: How to hand it back. Agree that they can stop at any time, no explanation needed. Knowing there is an exit makes people more willing to start.
00d0c275: Free to download, with one rule, one buddy and all three lock levels included.
f77a1255: Some people do not want the responsibility, and that is a reasonable answer. It is not a judgement of you. Ask someone else, or start with Medium lock — a five-minute enforced wait, no buddy required — and see how far that gets you. A fair number of people find they never need the stronger version.
c94ebfa0: Send them one short message: tell them whether it is working, and thank them. It costs you nothing and it is the difference between a buddy who stays engaged and one who quietly stops answering.
6ec8bd49: Then leave it alone. The system only works if you stop renegotiating it.
